title: Subqueries & CTEs
description: Nest queries inside queries, write correlated subqueries, name steps with WITH, and save queries as views

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.description: Use a query's result as the input to another query

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a subquery inside WHERE or FROM to answer a question that needs a two-step lookup.

sections.title: 🪆 A query inside a query
sections.content:
A **subquery** is a `SELECT` nested inside another query, usually to compute a value or a list the outer query needs. It runs first, and its result gets used by the outer query:

```sql
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
```

The inner query computes the average price once; the outer query then finds every product priced above that average. Notice the subquery is wrapped in parentheses — that's required.

sections.title: 📋 Subqueries returning a list, with IN
sections.content:
A subquery can also return a whole list of values, which pairs naturally with `IN`:

```sql
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total_amount > 500
);
```

This finds customers who have placed at least one order over $500 — the inner query builds the list of qualifying customer IDs, and the outer query filters against it.

sections.title: 🪑 Subqueries in FROM
sections.content:
A subquery can also stand in for a table, when you need to query the *result* of another query:

```sql
SELECT category, avg_price
FROM (
  SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category
) AS category_averages
WHERE avg_price > 50;
```

Here the inner query builds a small summary table on the fly, and the outer query treats it just like any other table — it even needs an alias (`AS category_averages`), same as a real table would.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the parentheses around a subquery. Using = with a subquery that can return more than one row (that requires IN, not =). Forgetting to alias a subquery used in FROM — most databases require it.

questions.question: What does WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) find?
options: Products priced exactly at the average
Products priced above the average price across all products
The single most expensive product
An error, since subqueries can't be used in WHERE
questions.explanation: The subquery computes one number — the average price — and the outer query keeps only products priced higher than that.

questions.question: Why does the customers-who-spent-over-$500 example use IN instead of =?
options: IN is required whenever a subquery is used
The subquery can return multiple customer_id values, and = only compares against a single value
= doesn't work with numbers
IN is just a stylistic preference with no functional difference
questions.explanation: = expects exactly one value on each side. Since multiple customers could have orders over $500, the subquery can return a list — which needs IN to check membership.

questions.question: When a subquery is used in FROM, what must it have?
options: Nothing extra — it works exactly like a table reference
An alias, since the outer query needs a name to refer to it by
A LIMIT clause
At least one JOIN inside it
questions.explanation: A subquery in FROM produces an unnamed result set, so SQL requires an alias (like AS category_averages) so the outer query can reference it.

questions.question: Where can a subquery legally appear in a SQL statement?
options: Only in WHERE
Only in SELECT
In WHERE, FROM, or SELECT, depending on what it returns
Only after ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Subqueries can appear in WHERE (as a filter), FROM (as a derived table), or SELECT (as a scalar value) — where you put it depends on what you need it to produce.

questions.question: What must a scalar subquery (used in SELECT or with =) return?
options: Multiple rows and columns
Exactly one row and one column
At least two rows
Nothing — it's optional
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery must resolve to a single value, so it needs to return exactly one row and one column, or the database raises an error.

questions.question: What happens if a subquery used with = unexpectedly returns more than one row?
options: The database picks the first row silently
The query raises a runtime error
It's automatically converted to IN
All rows are averaged together
questions.explanation: = expects a single value, so if the subquery returns multiple rows, most databases raise an error rather than guessing which one to use.

questions.question: Why is a subquery in FROM sometimes called a 'derived table'?
options: Because it modifies the original table
Because its result is treated like a temporary table the outer query can select from
Because it must be indexed
Because it deletes rows
questions.explanation: A subquery in FROM produces a result set that the outer query treats exactly like any other table — hence 'derived table'.

questions.question: Which is generally easier to read: a deeply nested subquery or breaking the logic into named CTEs?
options: Deeply nested subqueries are always easier
There's no readability difference
Named CTEs, since each step gets a clear label
Neither can be read by humans
questions.explanation: Naming each step as a CTE lets you read a query top-to-bottom in plain steps, instead of untangling nested parentheses inside-out.

lessons.title: Correlated Subqueries
lessons.description: Write a subquery that re-runs once per row of the outer query, using that row's own values

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what makes a subquery correlated, and write one that compares each row to its own group.

sections.title: 🔄 A subquery that depends on the outer row
sections.content:
The subqueries in the last lesson ran once, independently. A **correlated subquery** is different — it references a column from the outer query, so it effectively re-runs once *for every row* the outer query considers:

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount
FROM orders AS o
WHERE o.total_amount > (
  SELECT AVG(total_amount)
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id   -- refers to the outer row!
);
```

This finds orders that are **above that specific customer's own average** — not the store-wide average. Because the inner query references `o.customer_id` from the outer row, it computes a different average for every customer.

sections.title: 🆚 Correlated vs. plain subqueries
sections.content:
The distinction matters for both meaning and performance:

• A **plain subquery** runs once, produces a fixed value or list, and the outer query uses it
• A **correlated subquery** re-evaluates for each outer row, because it references that row's data

Correlated subqueries are more powerful — they can express "compare this row to its own group" — but they can also be slower on large tables, since the inner query conceptually runs many times.

sections.title: ✅ EXISTS: checking for at least one match
sections.content:
`EXISTS` is a common companion to correlated subqueries — it checks whether the inner query returns *any* row at all, without caring what the row contains:

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
```

This finds customers with at least one order — similar to the LEFT JOIN + IS NOT NULL pattern from the joins module, but expressed as a subquery instead.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing a correlated subquery when a simple JOIN + GROUP BY would answer the same question more clearly and often faster. Not noticing a subquery is correlated (missed the outer column reference), leading to confusion about why it's slow on a large table.

questions.question: What makes a subquery 'correlated'?
options: It uses the AVG function
It references a column from the outer query, so it conceptually re-runs per outer row
It's written in a FROM clause
It always returns exactly one row
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery references the outer query's current row (like o.customer_id), which means its result can differ for each row the outer query processes.

questions.question: In the correlated subquery example, what does the inner query compute for each order?
options: The store-wide average order amount
That specific customer's own average order amount
The number of orders total
The most recent order date
questions.explanation: Because the inner query filters WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id, it computes the average total_amount only for that one customer — a different value per customer.

questions.question: What does EXISTS check for?
options: That the subquery returns a specific value
Whether the subquery returns at least one row, regardless of its content
That a column is NOT NULL
That two tables have matching column names
questions.explanation: EXISTS only cares whether the inner query produces any rows at all — it's a yes/no check for "does at least one match exist", commonly used with correlated subqueries.

questions.question: Why can correlated subqueries be slower than uncorrelated ones on large tables?
options: They can't use indexes at all
They may conceptually re-execute once per outer row instead of once total
They always return more rows
They require a JOIN
questions.explanation: Because a correlated subquery depends on the outer row's value, the database may need to evaluate it once per outer row rather than just once, which can be costly on large tables.

questions.question: What's the difference between EXISTS and IN when checking for related rows?
options: They are identical in every case
EXISTS only checks for row presence and can stop at the first match; IN compares against a full list of values
IN is always faster
EXISTS requires a correlated subquery, IN never does
questions.explanation: EXISTS just asks 'is there at least one matching row?' and can short-circuit, while IN compares the outer value against a full set of returned values.

questions.question: What does NOT EXISTS let you find?
options: Rows where the subquery returns any result
Rows where the correlated subquery returns no matching rows
All rows in the outer table
Only NULL rows
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS is the inverse of EXISTS — it keeps outer rows for which the correlated subquery finds zero matching rows.

questions.question: In a correlated subquery, what makes the inner query dependent on the outer query?
options: It uses a JOIN keyword
It references a column from the outer query's current row
It contains an aggregate function
It has an ORDER BY clause
questions.explanation: Correlation happens when the inner query references a column from the outer row currently being evaluated, tying the two together.

questions.question: Can a correlated subquery be rewritten using a JOIN in many cases?
options: Never — they solve unrelated problems
Often yes, and the JOIN version may run faster since databases can optimize joins more directly
Only if it uses EXISTS
Only for DELETE statements
questions.explanation: Many correlated subquery patterns have an equivalent JOIN formulation, and query planners often optimize joins more efficiently than row-by-row correlated execution.

lessons.title: Common Table Expressions (WITH)
lessons.description: Name a subquery up front with WITH to make long queries readable

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Rewrite a nested subquery as a named CTE using WITH, and chain multiple CTEs together.

sections.title: 📛 Giving a subquery a name
sections.content:
A **Common Table Expression** (CTE) lets you define a subquery once, up front, with a name — then reference that name later in the query as if it were a real table. It's written with `WITH`:

```sql
WITH category_averages AS (
  SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category
)
SELECT category, avg_price
FROM category_averages
WHERE avg_price > 50;
```

This is exactly the same result as the FROM-subquery example from two lessons ago — but reads top-to-bottom instead of inside-out, which gets much easier to follow as queries grow.

sections.title: 🧱 Chaining multiple CTEs
sections.content:
You can define several CTEs in one query, each one able to reference the ones defined before it — useful for breaking a complex report into readable steps:

```sql
WITH big_spenders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 200
),
big_spender_details AS (
  SELECT c.name, bs.total_spent
  FROM big_spenders AS bs
  JOIN customers AS c ON bs.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM big_spender_details ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
```

Each CTE reads like a labeled step: first find the big spenders, then attach their names, then present the result.

sections.title: 💡 Why prefer CTEs over nested subqueries
sections.content: As queries grow, nested nested subqueries (a subquery inside a subquery inside a subquery) become hard to read from the inside out. CTEs solve this by naming each step and letting you read a query **top to bottom, like a recipe** — this is usually the single biggest readability upgrade you can make to a complex query.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the comma between multiple CTEs in the same WITH clause. Naming a CTE the same as a real table, which can be confusing even though it's technically allowed.

questions.question: What does a CTE (WITH ... AS (...)) let you do?
options: Permanently create a new table in the database
Name a subquery so it can be referenced later in the same query, like a temporary named result
Rename an existing column
Delete rows from a table
questions.explanation: A CTE defines a named, temporary result set that exists only for the duration of that one query — it doesn't persist in the database.

questions.question: Why are CTEs often easier to read than deeply nested subqueries?
options: They run faster in every database
They let you read the query top-to-bottom as a sequence of named steps, instead of inside-out
They eliminate the need for JOIN
They automatically remove duplicate rows
questions.explanation: Nested subqueries have to be read from the innermost query outward, which gets hard to follow. CTEs give each step a name and let the query read in a natural top-to-bottom order.

questions.question: In the chained-CTE example, what does big_spender_details reference?
options: The raw orders table directly
The big_spenders CTE defined earlier in the same WITH clause
A completely separate query
Nothing — it's independent of big_spenders
questions.explanation: CTEs defined later in the same WITH clause can reference CTEs defined earlier, letting you build a multi-step chain of named intermediate results.

questions.question: Does a CTE persist after the query that defines it finishes?
options: Yes, permanently, like a table
No — it only exists for the duration of that single query
Yes, until the database restarts
Only if explicitly saved
questions.explanation: A CTE is scoped to the single statement that defines it; once that query finishes, the CTE is gone.

questions.question: Can you reference an earlier CTE from a later CTE in the same WITH clause?
options: No, CTEs can't reference each other
Yes — a later CTE can build on an earlier one, letting you chain steps
Only if they have the same name
Only in a subquery, never a CTE
questions.explanation: CTEs can be chained: a later CTE in the same WITH clause can select from an earlier one, letting you build up a multi-step transformation.

questions.question: What is a recursive CTE typically used for?
options: Formatting query output
Working with hierarchical or graph-like data, such as an org chart or category tree
Only counting rows
Encrypting data
questions.explanation: Recursive CTEs repeatedly reference themselves to walk hierarchical structures like org charts, folder trees, or bill-of-materials data.

questions.question: How does a CTE differ from a temporary table created with CREATE TEMP TABLE?
options: They are exactly the same thing
A CTE is defined inline and scoped to one query; a temp table persists across multiple statements in a session
CTEs can only hold numbers
Temp tables can't be queried with SELECT
questions.explanation: A CTE only exists within the query where it's written, while a temp table sticks around across multiple statements until dropped or the session ends.

questions.question: What's a practical reason to use a CTE instead of just adding another JOIN?
options: CTEs are required by SQL standard for any JOIN
When the intermediate result involves aggregation or filtering that's clearer as a separate named step
CTEs eliminate the need for WHERE
There's no difference
questions.explanation: When an intermediate step needs its own grouping, filtering, or calculation, giving it a name as a CTE keeps the overall query understandable instead of piling logic into one JOIN.

lessons.title: Views
lessons.description: Save a query as a reusable virtual table

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a view is, create one, and query it like a regular table.

sections.title: 🪟 A saved query you can reuse
sections.content:
A **view** is a query saved under a name in the database, so anyone can query it later just like a real table — but it doesn't store its own copy of the data. Every time you query a view, the underlying query runs fresh against the real tables.

```sql
CREATE VIEW customer_spending AS
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
```

Now, anyone can simply run `SELECT * FROM customer_spending WHERE total_spent > 500;` without needing to know or repeat the join and grouping logic.

sections.title: 🆚 Views vs. CTEs
sections.content:
Both name a query for reuse, but at different scopes:

• A **CTE** exists only inside the one query it's defined in
• A **view** is saved in the database and can be reused by any future query, by anyone with access

Think of a CTE as a local variable for one query, and a view as a shared, named query the whole team can rely on.

sections.title: 💡 Why views are useful
sections.content:
Views are especially handy for:

• Hiding complex joins behind a simple name, so others don't need to re-derive the logic
• Presenting a consistent, agreed-upon definition of something like "active customers" everywhere it's used
• Restricting which columns or rows someone sees, without touching the underlying tables

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Expecting a view to be faster than the original query — it isn't, since it re-runs the same underlying logic every time. Forgetting that a view reflects live data, not a frozen snapshot from when it was created.

questions.question: What does a view actually store?
options: A permanent copy of the query's results, frozen at creation time
The query itself — it re-runs against the real tables every time the view is queried
Nothing; it's purely documentation
A compressed version of the underlying tables
questions.explanation: A view stores the query definition, not a data snapshot. Every time you SELECT from a view, the saved query runs fresh against the current data.

questions.question: What's the key difference in scope between a CTE and a view?
options: There is no difference
A CTE only exists within the single query that defines it; a view is saved and reusable by any future query
Views can only be used once, CTEs can be reused forever
CTEs require admin permissions, views don't
questions.explanation: A CTE is local to the one WITH...query it's part of. A view is a persistent, named object in the database that any query can reference later.

questions.question: Why might a team create a customer_spending view instead of repeating the join+GROUP BY everywhere?
options: Views run instantly with no computation
It gives everyone one agreed-upon, reusable definition instead of each person re-deriving the same logic
It's required by SQL syntax
It automatically updates the underlying tables
questions.explanation: A view centralizes a query's logic under one name, so everyone queries the same well-defined thing instead of subtly different copies of similar logic scattered across many queries.

questions.question: If the underlying table changes, does a view reflect those changes the next time it's queried?
options: No, views are frozen snapshots
Yes, since a view re-runs its defining query against current data every time
Only after manually refreshing the view
Only for numeric columns
questions.explanation: A standard view stores only the query definition, not the data, so it always reflects the current state of the underlying tables when queried.

questions.question: What's one reason to create a view around a complex join?
options: It permanently speeds up all future queries
It hides the complexity so other users can query a simple, consistent name
It's required before you can use GROUP BY
It automatically creates indexes
questions.explanation: A view lets you package a complex join or calculation behind a simple, reusable name so other users don't need to re-derive that logic themselves.

questions.question: Can you typically query a view the same way you'd query a regular table?
options: No, views need special syntax
Yes — you can SELECT from a view just like a table, with WHERE, JOIN, etc.
Only with INSERT statements
Only if it has no WHERE clause
questions.explanation: From the querying side, a view behaves like a regular table: you can SELECT, filter, and join against it normally.

questions.question: What is a materialized view, in contrast to a regular view?
options: Exactly the same as a regular view
A view whose results are physically stored and must be refreshed periodically, trading freshness for speed
A view that can never be queried
A view limited to one column
questions.explanation: A materialized view stores its computed result physically on disk rather than recomputing it every time, which is faster to read but needs periodic refreshing to stay current.

questions.question: Why might exposing a view instead of the raw tables help with security or simplicity?
options: Views can't be created by regular users
A view can expose only specific columns or rows, hiding sensitive or irrelevant data from consumers
Views automatically encrypt all data
There is no benefit
questions.explanation: A view can select only the columns and rows a consumer needs, so it can restrict what's visible without changing permissions on the underlying tables.
